result.summary: Pindar opens by asking which of Thebes' glorious deeds pleased her most, listing the births of Dionysos and Herakles and other Theban heroes. He then celebrates Strepsiades, a pankratiast victor at the Isthmus, and his namesake uncle who died in battle. He ends with a warning against reaching for the gods' heights, citing Bellerophon, and a prayer to Apollo.

scenes.title: Editor's note on date
scenes.summary: The editor says the ode's date is uncertain and links it conjecturally to the battle of Oinophyta.

scenes.title: Glories of Thebes
scenes.summary: Pindar asks Thebe which of her famous deeds pleased her most, recalling Dionysos, Herakles, Teiresias, Adrastos and the Spartoi. He notes that old glory sleeps unless song preserves it.
scenes.stakes: Old glory is forgotten unless kept alive by song.

scenes.title: Strepsiades and his uncle
scenes.summary: Pindar praises Strepsiades' Isthmian pankration victory and shares the glory with his uncle, who died fighting for his country.
scenes.stakes: The uncle gave his life in battle; renown is the recompense.

scenes.title: Calm, mortality, Bellerophon, prayer
scenes.summary: Pindar says his grief has passed, warns against aiming at the gods' realm using Bellerophon, and prays Apollo for a Pythian crown.
scenes.stakes: Overreaching mortals meet a bitter end, as Bellerophon was thrown.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of Apollo, god of Pytho and the Pythian games.
Epithet of Poseidon, lord of the Isthmian games.

notable_quotes.reason: A plain statement of human mortality despite differing fortunes.
Song alone preserves the glory of the past.

analysis.text: Song gives lasting fame to deeds, and heroic death in defence of one's city earns renown for both the dead and the community.
The Bellerophon example teaches mortals to accept limits and not strive for the gods' realm.

legacy.text: Bellerophon's fall on Pegasos became a lasting image of human pride and overreach in later literature.

fun_facts.text: The editor notes that the date is uncertain and the link to Oinophyta (457 BC) is only a guess.

language_notes.text: "Wherewithal of" means roughly "in which of"; Pindar asks which of Thebe's fine deeds pleased her most.
Zeus came to Alkmene, Amphitryon's wife, in a night of golden snow, disguised as her husband, and so fathered Herakles.
The Spartoi, "sown men", sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Kadmos and became ancestors of Theban nobility.
"Iris-haired" refers to the Muses' violet or rainbow-coloured hair, a conventional epithet.
"Earth-grasper" translates a title of Poseidon, the earth-holder, who is god of the Isthmian games.
Bellerophon tried to ride the winged horse Pegasos to Olympos and was thrown for his presumption.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, god of prophecy.

context_notes.text: Oinophyta was a battle in which Athens defeated the Boiotians, including Thebes, in 457 B.C.
The pankration combined wrestling and boxing, and was among the toughest events at the Isthmian games.
Meleagros, Hektor and Amphiaraos are legendary warriors; Pindar compares the dead uncle with them.

literary_notes.text: Pindar addresses Thebe, the city personified as a goddess, opening the ode by speaking directly to her.
Song is imagined as a spouse to whom a man is married, giving him the lasting reward of fame.
Grief is a storm and renewed joy is a calm after it.
Bellerophon serves as a mythic warning example, illustrating the limits of mortal ambition.
